newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey stock market eyes economic reforms in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Turkey stock market eyes economic reforms in 1997.

text.p: Performance in the Turkish stock market will mainly depend on the degree of confidence gained from the government's long-awaited structural economic reforms in 1997, brokers and analysts said.

They said no steps were taken to reform the economy in 1996, which was described as a year of political instability amid efforts to form a lasting government after inconclusive general elections held on December 24, 1995.
The market's hopes for 1997 are primarily set on privatisation.

"Income from privatisation will not begin to flow in from January 2, 1997, but what we need is to feel confident that the structural measures in the economy started to be taken," said Tayyar Ozturk, general manager of Ekinciler securities.
The goverment has targeted a zero-deficit budget for 1997 after an expected 1,300 trillion lira ($12.1 billion) deficit this year.
The 6,255-trillion-lira 1997 budget, published in the official gazette on Thursday, aims to collect 70 percent of revenues from taxes and the rest from non-tax items led by privatisation revenues.

If the goverment fails to meet its 1997 targets, brokers foresee interest rates rising, maturity periods shortening and so returns on stock investments remaining below inflation. The official 1997 inflation target is 65 percent, after an expected rate of around 80 percent this year.
"Next year it will become clear how realistic the goverment's economic targets are," said Alp Tekince, acting chairman of Bumerang securities.
Ozturk from Ekinciler said the stock market index might surge beyond the 200,000 level if the targets were realised, but added that such a breakthrough was seen unlikely.

The composite market index gained 143 percent from end-1995 to an all-time high close of 97,425.62 on Thursday, but in dollar terms it stood at 91 cents, compared to a $1 record on April 8 and up 35.8 percent from $0.67 at the end of last year.

"Investors made good returns from the stock market in 1996, but it is hard for it to become better in 1997. I would look at individual sectors rather than the index itself next year," said Atilla Koksal, assistant general manager at Interbank.
Brokers warned that main economic problems -- huge budget and trade deficits and hefty domestic debt -- were being delayed and new borrowing instruments were only temporary solutions.

Turkey will launch a new domestic borrowing instrument in 1997 with a return covering inflation plus risk premium after selling $2 billion of foreign currency-denominated, three-year bonds to Turkish banks since September.
Some brokers also expressed concern on the possibility of political uncertainty in 1997, which could batter the economy.

"I think the existing static political atmosphere will fade away in 1997. There might be problems in foreign relations and the coalition's progress, thus political and international relations may influence the market more," said Resat Kutucular from Toros securities.
New regulations announced by the Capital Markets Board and the Exchange on tightening market supervision are also seen as factors likely to affect trade from the first week of 1997.
"The new regulations will reduce trade volume but the market will be more consistent," said Ozturk from Ekinciler.

Ozturk, who described the listed companies as those that can adjust themselves more easily to political and economic turbulance, said the companies increased their profits and improved their ability to manage at a time of economic problems in the past two years, particularly during the 1994 financial crisis.
